content: We appreciate your time and willingness to share deeply personal experiences, thoughts, and feelings. Once all the data is collected, it will be analyzed, and a report will be prepared and sent to you, likely by early March 2014. Please note that no identifying information about you will be included in the report. Would you like to receive a copy of the report via email? Additionally, would you mind if we contacted you later for any follow-up questions? You can indicate your preference by selecting Yes or No. Participant Information Sheet: Verbal Informed Consent for Participation in the Study on Transgender People and HIV We are conducting interviews with transgender men and women to better understand their experiences and needs related to HIV and other health issues. This information sheet provides a detailed explanation of the interview process. Before the phone interview, the interviewer will verbally explain this information to you again. You are encouraged to ask any questions about the interview process that you do not fully understand. Once you understand all aspects of the interview, you can decide whether or not to participate. If you agree to participate verbally, we will provide you with a written copy of this information sheet for your records. Please note that your participation is entirely voluntary, and you are not obligated to take part if you do not wish to. Purpose of the Interviews The World Health Organization (WHO) HIV Department is conducting these interviews to gain a deeper understanding of the HIV-related needs of transgender individuals worldwide. Specifically, the study aims to explore HIV-related risk behaviors, experiences with healthcare services, and the challenges and opportunities for effective HIV prevention, treatment, and care among transgender people. The findings will help WHO develop recommendations for HIV guidance tailored to key populations, including transgender individuals. Why You Were Invited You are being asked to participate because you are a transgender individual who expressed interest in being interviewed by completing our recent online survey titled Transgender People Short Survey. Number of Participants Approximately 20 transgender individuals will participate in this study. What Happens If You Agree to Participate If you agree to participate: 1. You will provide a phone number or Skype account name where you can be reached, along with a convenient date and time for the interview. 2. The interviewer will call you at the agreed-upon time and conduct a semi-structured interview lasting about one hour. The interviewer will ask guiding questions and allow you to freely discuss topics that are important to you. 3. The interview will be voice-recorded and transcribed. Only the interviewer will have access to the file linking your ID number to your name. 4. The transcribed interviews will be analyzed, and a report will be written and published. The report will include direct quotes from your interview and others, but no identifying information will be included. Risks of Participation There are some potential risks or discomforts associated with participating in this study. The interview includes personal questions about your past and current sexual activity, drug use, and transitioning experiences, which may make you feel shy or uncomfortable. You are not required to answer any questions you do not wish to and can simply decline to respond during the interview. Benefits of Participation There are no direct benefits to you for participating in this study. However, your participation will help WHO better understand how transgender individuals are affected by HIV and other health issues, which can inform improved HIV prevention, treatment, and care strategies. Privacy and Confidentiality While participation in research may involve some loss of privacy, your information will be handled as confidentially as possible. A study file with your interview ID number will be created electronically, and the recording and transcript of the interview will be stored in this file. Only the research team will have access to this file. After the analysis is completed, all personal identifying information and interview recordings will be deleted. The transcribed interviews will be stored electronically and used in the published report. Any published information will not include your name or other personal identifying details. Compensation You will not receive any payment for participating in this interview. Duration of the Interview If you decide to participate, the interview will take approximately 60 minutes (1 hour). Voluntary Participation Participation in this study is entirely voluntary. You may choose to participate or decline without any penalty. If you decide to participate, you can withdraw from the interview at any time without explanation or consequences. Participation is voluntary, and you can decline to participate at any point without any penalty or loss of rights. Annex 4: Health Interventions for Prisoners – Update on Literature Since 2007 HIV remains a significant issue in prison settings, with prevalence rates higher than in the general population, though these rates vary geographically. Most prisoners living with HIV or AIDS contract the infection outside of prison, but the risk of transmission within prisons is high due to behaviors such as sharing contaminated injecting equipment and unprotected sex. High-risk behaviors, including injection drug use, sexual activity, and tattooing or body piercing, are widespread in prisons, contributing to the transmission of HIV and hepatitis C (HCV). Studies have shown that HIV prevention programs, including education, condom distribution, opioid substitution therapy (OST), and needle and syringe programs (NSPs), can be successfully implemented in prisons and other closed settings. A comprehensive literature review conducted in 2007 highlighted the effectiveness of these interventions. An updated review in 2014, focusing on materials developed between 2007 and 2014, reaffirmed the findings of the 2007 review and emphasized the need for continued research in this area. Condom Distribution in Prisons Evidence indicates that providing condoms in prisons is feasible and does not disrupt prison routines, compromise security, or increase sexual activity or drug use. Water-based lubricants should also be provided to reduce the risk of condom breakage and rectal tearing, which can contribute to HIV transmission. Education and informational activities for both prisoners and staff should precede the introduction of condom distribution programs. Drug Dependence Treatment Opioid substitution therapy (OST) with methadone has been shown to be effective in reducing injecting drug use, needle sharing, and associated infections in prison settings. OST also facilitates the delivery of antiretroviral therapy for people who inject drugs. Other forms of drug dependence treatment, while less studied, have the potential to improve prisoner health, reduce reoffending, and enhance prison security. HIV/AIDS Education Well-designed HIV/AIDS education programs can improve prisoners' knowledge about HIV and related issues. Peer-led education programs are particularly effective in reaching prisoners. These findings underscore the importance of implementing evidence-based interventions in prison settings to address the unique challenges of HIV prevention, treatment, and care among incarcerated populations.
